name: Zoom
whyPeoplePay: Zoom sells a call that connects. Their bandwidth, their global relay network, their client on every laptop and phone and conference-room screen your guests already have, and a dial-in number for the person whose wifi has given up. The 40-minute limit on the free tier is the product working exactly as designed: it is short enough to interrupt a real meeting and long enough to prove the thing is good.

plans.name: Basic
plans.note: Free. Zoom's pricing page states 40 minutes per meeting and up to 100 participants.

plans.name: Pro
plans.note: Per user per month billed monthly; about $13.33 per user per month billed annually. Zoom's page states 30-hour meetings and up to 100 participants. See pricing.note: the vendor page did not render a figure to us and one secondary source lists the monthly rate as $18.33.

plans.name: Business
plans.note: Per user per month billed monthly; about $18.33 per user per month billed annually. Zoom's page states up to 300 participants.

plans.name: Enterprise
plans.note: Quote only. Zoom's page states up to 1000 participants.

pricing.note: Zoom's own pricing page renders its plan names, meeting lengths and participant caps as text, and those are what we recorded from it, but the dollar figures are drawn in by a script we could not read. The prices here come from two secondary trackers read on the same day, which agree on Business at $21.99 monthly and $18.33 annually and on Pro at $13.33 annually, and disagree on Pro billed monthly ($16.99 against $18.33). We recorded the lower of the two. Treat every figure on this page as needing a re-check against a signed-in Zoom checkout.

ranked.rationale: The only one here that a guest can join by clicking a link in a browser, with no account, no download and no explaining. That is the property Zoom actually sells, and it is the one that decides whether a self-hosted meeting server survives contact with people who did not choose it. What you take on in exchange is the bandwidth: your VPS relays every stream, so call quality stops being someone else's problem and becomes a line on your hosting bill.

evaluatedNotTested.name: BigBlueButton
evaluatedNotTested.note: Built for teaching, not for meetings: breakout rooms, a shared whiteboard, polls and a hand-raise queue, with learning-platform integrations as the point. Actively developed and LGPL-3.0. It is also much heavier than Jitsi, expects a dedicated machine running a specific Ubuntu release, and installs through its own script rather than a compose file, which is why it is not the pick for someone replacing a Zoom Pro seat.

evaluatedNotTested.name: Galene
evaluatedNotTested.note: A single Go binary under MIT, maintained and deliberately small: one process, no XMPP server, no Java, and it runs usefully on hardware that Jitsi would struggle on. The trade is polish and reach. Fewer client features, a plainer interface, and a much smaller pool of people who have hit your problem before. Worth a serious look if the box is tiny.

evaluatedNotTested.name: LiveKit
evaluatedNotTested.note: Apache-2.0, very actively developed, and the wrong shape for this page: it is a WebRTC server and SDK you build a product on, not a meeting product you can hand a link to. There is a sample conferencing app, but choosing LiveKit means committing to writing and hosting the front end yourself.
